trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the Highline Trail from Logan Pass typically stays closed by lingering snow into early-to-mid July even after Going-to-the-Sun Road fully opens, so check the park's current trail status page before planning a Logan Pass start.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail's first mile hugs a ledge above the Going-to-the-Sun Road with a fixed cable handhold bolted into the cliff, added after early visitors found the exposure too intimidating.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the trail beyond Hidden Lake Overlook is periodically closed to protect bears and other wildlife feeding in the area, especially in late summer — the boardwalk and overlook segment from Logan Pass typically stays open even when the descent to the lakeshore is closed.
trails.didYouKnow: The overlook sits directly on the Continental Divide, and on a clear day you can see peaks in both Glacier and Canada's Waterton Lakes National Park.

trails.trailTip: The trail follows Avalanche Creek's cedar-lined gorge before climbing to the lake basin — arrive early since this is one of the busiest trailhead parking areas in the park by mid-morning.
trails.didYouKnow: Avalanche Lake sits in a glacially carved cirque fed by several waterfalls tumbling off the Sperry Glacier's remnant ice above.

trails.trailTip: The Many Glacier valley has some of the park's highest grizzly activity, so hike in a group, make noise, and carry bear spray; a concessioner boat shuttle across Swiftcurrent and Josephine lakes can shorten the round trip by several miles if you'd rather skip the flat valley approach.
trails.didYouKnow: The turquoise color of Grinnell Glacier's meltwater lake comes from finely ground "glacial flour" rock particles suspended in the water.

trails.trailTip: A flat, wheelchair-accessible boardwalk loop through old-growth cedar and hemlock — a good option for a short leg-stretch on the drive along Going-to-the-Sun Road.
trails.didYouKnow: This pocket of cedar-hemlock rainforest exists because moist Pacific air funnels up the McDonald Creek valley, creating a microclimate very different from the drier forests elsewhere in the park.

trails.trailTip: This trail passes through dense berry-producing shrubs that draw grizzlies in late summer, so hike with a group, make noise on blind corners, and carry bear spray; icebergs can persist on the lake into August in a heavy snow year.
trails.didYouKnow: Iceberg Lake sits in such a deep, shaded cirque that chunks of winter ice can survive floating on its surface well into summer.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this high traverse from the Siyeh Bend trailhead along Going-to-the-Sun Road typically isn't fully snow-free until mid-to-late July, and lingering snowfields near the pass can make footing hazardous even after the road opens for the season.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail crosses Siyeh Pass at over 8,000 feet, one of the highest maintained trail crossings in the park, with views into both the St. Mary and Baring Creek valleys.

trails.trailTip: A short, mostly flat walk near Two Medicine to a unique waterfall where two streams appear to merge mid-fall — an easy stop for all ages and abilities.
trails.didYouKnow: Running Eagle Falls is nicknamed "Trick Falls" because in high water an upper falls appears to emerge from partway up the cliff, fed by an underground channel through the limestone.

animals.whereToLook: High alpine meadows and berry patches near Many Glacier, Two Medicine, and the Highline Trail
animals.viewingTip: Keep at least 100 yards between yourself and any grizzly, view and photograph with binoculars or a zoom lens, carry bear spray and know how to use it, and never approach a bear feeding on berries or a carcass.
animals.didYouKnow: Glacier's grizzlies can pack on several pounds a day during late-summer hyperphagia, gorging on huckleberries before den-up in November.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky slopes and ledges along the Highline Trail and Logan Pass
animals.viewingTip: Goats at Logan Pass are used to people and may approach you seeking salt from sweat or urine — back away if one approaches, never let a goat lick your skin or gear, and never urinate near the trail, since habituated goats have become aggressive enough to be a real safety issue here.
animals.didYouKnow: Mountain goats aren't true goats but are more closely related to antelope, and their split, rubbery hooves act almost like suction cups on wet rock.

animals.whereToLook: Remote forested valleys away from main trail corridors
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are rare and brief — enjoy them through binoculars from wherever you are and never approach a den or rendezvous site if you locate one, since disturbance can cause a pack to abandon pups.
animals.didYouKnow: Wolves recolonized Glacier naturally from Canada in the 1980s, decades before the more famous reintroduction to Yellowstone.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky slopes near Logan Pass and Grinnell Point
animals.viewingTip: Use binoculars to watch from a distance, and give extra space in late spring and early summer when ewes are with newborn lambs on steep terrain that leaves little room to safely move away from people.
animals.didYouKnow: Bighorn rams' curled horns can weigh up to 30 pounds, more than all the bones in their body combined.

animals.whereToLook: Willow-lined wetlands, including Fishercap Lake near Many Glacier
animals.viewingTip: Stay at least 25 yards away and give considerably more room during the fall rut — moose are responsible for more close-encounter injuries in the park than bears, and a moose with pinned-back ears or raised hackles needs you to retreat immediately.
animals.didYouKnow: Moose are strong swimmers and will dive completely underwater to reach aquatic plants at the bottom of shallow lakes like Fishercap.

animals.whereToLook: Rockslides and talus along the Highline and Grinnell Glacier trails
animals.viewingTip: Watch and photograph marmots from the trail rather than approaching a rockslide colony, and never feed them — human food disrupts their fat reserves needed for an eight-month hibernation.
animals.didYouKnow: Hoary marmots are named for their frosted, silver-gray fur and are sometimes called "whistlers" for their sharp alarm calls, which lent their name to Whistler, British Columbia.

animals.whereToLook: Remote high-alpine basins, rarely seen by day hikers
animals.viewingTip: A wolverine sighting is a rare privilege — watch from as far away as your optics allow and never try to approach or track one toward a snow den, since female wolverines are extremely sensitive to disturbance while raising kits.
animals.didYouKnow: Glacier is a stronghold for wolverine research in the Lower 48; females dig natal dens into deep spring snowpack that can persist into early summer.

animals.whereToLook: Mountain passes such as Mount Brown Lookout and Lincoln Pass during fall migration
animals.viewingTip: Watch migrating eagles ride ridge thermals from an overlook with binoculars — the birds pass at a distance naturally, so there's no need to approach a perch or nesting cliff to get a good look.
animals.didYouKnow: Glacier's high passes funnel one of the largest golden eagle migrations in the Lower 48 each autumn, drawing citizen-science hawk counts at established lookout points.
